title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
gist: WIRED guide (republished by Ars Technica) arguing that a cluster of US IT outages in four business days (Microsoft Exchange, FAA, JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, NSA network) shows no evidence of hacking, and laying out a five-step method for distinguishing cyberattacks from ordinary outages: presume accident, check status pages, use network data, look for claims of responsibility, and wait.

insights.claim: Within four consecutive US business days, a Microsoft Exchange outage, an FAA tech failure grounding flights, a JPMorgan Chase software problem, a United Airlines system glitch and an NSA classified-network outage occurred, with no evidence any were related or caused by hackers.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Clustered infrastructure outages are not by themselves a signal of coordinated cyberwar; avoid trading on attack narratives without evidence.
insights.locator: Across just four consecutive business days

insights.claim: The perception of a coordinated cyberattack behind the US outage cluster was amplified by context: an ongoing US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Geopolitical tension raises the market's propensity to misattribute routine outages to attacks, creating overreaction risk.
insights.locator: In the midst of a US war with Iran

insights.claim: Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince says most current outages are standard background noise from complex systems breaking, not cyberattacks.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Infrastructure providers view outage frequency as structural complexity risk rather than a security escalation.
insights.quote: Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.
insights.locator: I’ve just seen enough times where we thought

insights.claim: Infoblox head of Internet analysis Doug Madory monitors up to a dozen network outages a day and estimates only about one in a thousand is caused by hackers.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A ~0.1% attack base rate means the default prior on any outage should be accident, not breach.
insights.quote: “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,”
insights.locator: 1. Start with a presumption of innocence

insights.claim: According to IPinfo's João Tomé, most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted, typically from a bad update, configuration change, cable cut or power failure.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Operational/change-management failures are the dominant outage risk for cloud and enterprise IT vendors.
insights.quote: “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,”

insights.claim: Outage duration is a diagnostic: a faulty-update rollback takes minutes or hours, while ransomware disruptions take days or weeks.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Watch outage length to infer cause; multi-day outages raise the probability of a breach with longer business impact.
insights.locator: Aside from the time it takes for companies

insights.claim: Doug Madory argues that clustered outages reflect increasing technology complexity and society's total dependence on Internet services, and that outages will never be completely eliminated.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Resilience, observability and redundancy spending is a durable need because outages are a permanent feature of Internet-mediated society.
insights.quote: “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through Internet-based services.
insights.locator: For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages

insights.claim: Downtime at a foundational provider such as Amazon Web Services can cascade into failures across its many dependent customers, making many sites appear down at once.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler concentration means a single provider incident creates correlated, economy-wide outage risk.
insights.locator: In the scramble to understand what’s really happening

insights.claim: The week's apparent multi-bank outage seems to have stemmed from inter-institutional transactions involving JPMorgan Chase rather than separate failures at multiple banks.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Payment-network interdependence lets one bank's software issue look like a sector-wide outage.
insights.locator: In other cases, multiple services can seem

insights.claim: AWS, Google Cloud Platform and Microsoft Azure all publish status dashboard pages, which along with verified company accounts and newsrooms are the primary sources for confirming outage scope and restoration.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Status dashboards are the first-line, real-time data source for monitoring vendor incidents.
insights.locator: Another concrete and vital source of information

insights.claim: Georgia Tech's IODA, Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net provide broad Internet monitoring data whose scope, location and timing can point to causes such as buggy updates, fiber cuts, cyberattacks or government shutdowns.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Third-party Internet measurement services are useful independent signals for outage attribution.
insights.locator: 3. Check trusted sources of network data

insights.claim: Ransomware gangs, the most common source of serious malicious Internet disruption, usually publicize breaches on dark-web extortion sites, sometimes with countdown timers to pressure victims.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Dark-web leak-site postings are a leading indicator that an outage is a breach rather than an accident.
insights.locator: Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source

insights.claim: Hacker claims of responsibility are unreliable since groups exaggerate or lie, and some major attacks such as the 2016 Mirai attack on Dyn came with no public claim at all.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Neither the presence nor absence of a hacker claim is conclusive; weight it as one data point.

insights.claim: Official confirmation of cyberattacks from agencies like CISA or private threat-intelligence firms can take days, weeks or even months, so patience is the best approach when evidence is thin.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Expect long lags before attribution; early rumor-driven moves are prone to reversal.
